opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's mostly pattern matching from about a decade of watching this exact story play out in image classifiers. Adversarial training is a real, good technique; it's one of the few things that has held up at all. But it only really works when the attacks you train against are representative of the attacks you'll actually face. You're optimizing to be robust to a particular distribution of attacks, and the model gets very good at resisting precisely those.

With TAR, the setting is: you release weights, and you want the model to resist someone fine-tuning it to recover harmful capabilities. So during training you simulate a bunch of fine-tuning attacks and teach the model to resist them. The problem is that the space of possible fine-tuning procedures is enormous. Different learning rates, optimizers, datasets, schedules, LoRA versus full fine-tuning, a few steps of something weird first. The attacker controls all of that and gets to choose after seeing your defense. That's the worst possible position for a defender.

What tends to happen is that the defense doesn't make the bad capability go away. It makes the loss landscape locally nasty, so the standard gradient-based fine-tuning they tested gets stuck or diverges. That looks great in the evaluation table. But it's basically gradient masking under a new name, and we know that story: you change the attack slightly, warm up differently, use a different optimizer, and suddenly you're past the bumpy region and the capability comes right back.

So my prior was that if the knowledge is still in the weights, and it almost certainly is, then some reasonable variation on fine-tuning the authors didn't train against would recover it. And that's more or less what happened. It wasn't some brilliant new attack. It was trying the things a careful adversary would obviously try. To be clear, I think it's an important problem and I'm glad people are working on it. But the bar for "this resists a motivated attacker with full weight access" is extremely high, and evaluating against your own attacks almost never clears it.

r001.rationale: The response says TAR trains against a limited set of fine-tuning attacks, while an attacker can vary the procedure and get past the resulting defense.

r002.rationale: It compares TAR’s defense to past adversarial-training failures in image classifiers, but does not state that TAR used one-step adversarial training.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't anything specific to that paper. It's the base rate. I've been doing this for about ten years now, and in that time the pattern has been remarkably consistent: a paper comes out claiming some kind of robustness, people get excited, and then a few weeks or months later it turns out the evaluation just wasn't adversarial enough. The defenses that have actually held up, you can count on one hand. So when a new one shows up, my prior isn't "this is probably broken," it's "this is almost certainly broken, and my job is to figure out how."

The TAR case specifically, the thing that made me more confident, was that they were trying to do something I think is genuinely very hard. The claim was tamper resistance, meaning you release the open weights and even if someone fine-tunes the model, they can't recover the dangerous capability. That's a much stronger property than ordinary adversarial robustness. With input-space attacks, the attacker only gets to change the pixels or the tokens. Here the attacker gets to change every single parameter in the model. You're giving them the whole thing. The intuition that should make you nervous is: the knowledge is still in there somewhere, because the model has to be useful for the stuff you want it to do, and the attacker has gradient access to all of it. It's hard to see how you hide something from someone who can rewrite you.

And then the specific mechanism they used, adversarial training over the fine-tuning process, has a familiar weakness. You train against the attacks you can imagine and simulate during training. The attacker gets to show up afterwards and do something you didn't simulate. In the image domain we learned this over and over: train against PGD with one set of hyperparameters, and someone comes along with a slightly different optimizer, or a different learning rate, or just more steps, and the robustness disappears. There's no reason the fine-tuning setting should be different. If anything it's worse, because the space of possible fine-tuning procedures is enormous.

So when we actually sat down to break it, the attacks weren't clever. That's the point I'd want people to take away. Change the learning rate schedule, change which parameters you update, run it longer, try a few variations. Most of the robustness went away. Not because the authors did something foolish, but because the evaluation that gets you to a paper deadline is almost never as thorough as the one an actual adversary runs when they have a month and a motive.

r001.rationale: It says training against attacks that are simulated can leave the defense vulnerable to attacks with different settings or more steps, causing robustness to disappear.

r002.rationale: It compares TAR’s adversarial-training weakness to failed image-domain defenses, but does not identify TAR’s training as one-step adversarial training.

astra-6.text:
My prior is that adversarial training is very hard to get right. You train against a particular set of attacks, and then the question is whether you’ve learned to defend against the underlying problem or just against those particular attacks. Often, a new attack finds something the training procedure missed.

So seeing adversarial training in the defense wasn’t, by itself, a reason to believe it would fail. But it made me want to look closely at the gap between what the defender trained against and what an attacker was actually allowed to do. The defender needs to cover that whole space; I only need to find one strategy that works. That asymmetry is why I was skeptical.

r001.rationale: The response says training against particular attacks can miss the underlying problem, allowing a new attack to find a vulnerability. This conveys that limited attacks can leave a defense vulnerable to stronger or unseen attacks.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention one-step adversarial training or compare TAR with previously failed defenses in image classification.

sol-6.1.text:
My prior was that adversarial training is very good at making a model robust to the attacks you train against, but that’s different from making it robust to every attack someone might come up with. The hard part is knowing whether your attacks are actually strong enough. If an attack fails, did the defense work, or did your optimization just fail to find a way around it?

For TAR, the attacker gets to modify the model’s weights. That’s a very powerful capability, and the defense is trained against a particular collection of ways of doing that, with a limited amount of compute. I expected there would be other ways to fine-tune the model, or different optimization choices, that weren’t covered by that training procedure. So my expectation wasn’t that adversarial training had accomplished nothing. It was that the robustness would be narrower than the claim you’d ultimately want: that someone who has the weights can’t undo the safety training.

r001.rationale: The response says adversarial training may cover only the attacks used in training and that other, stronger optimization approaches could bypass the defense.

r002.rationale: It does not mention one-step adversarial training or compare TAR to previously failed adversarial training defenses in image classification.
